Caio, thanks for making the time. I have read the one-pager, so I will skip the introductions. How long has the forecasting engine been in production?
Two years. We have been building it since 2022, and it has been live with clients for the last fourteen months.
And it is proprietary? Nothing licensed underneath it?
Entirely ours. That is the part of the business we would not sell separately.
Right. Now, the growth. Your pipeline — has it been growing evenly, or did you have one very good quarter that is doing all the work?
It has been growing every quarter since March. No single quarter carries it, and no single client is more than eight percent.

That is the answer I was hoping for. I should say, our due diligence is fairly unforgiving, so if anything is going to look awkward in the data room, I would rather hear it from you now than find it in week three.

I have sat through a lot of first months, and founders make the same three mistakes in almost the same order. The first one is answering a question they have not checked. Somebody asks what the renewal rate is, the founder says ninety-two off the top of his head, and three weeks later the data room says eighty-seven. Nobody thinks he lied. Everybody stops trusting the next number. The correction always costs more than the delay would have. The second mistake is waiting on bad news, hoping it will look smaller once the growth numbers land. It never does. It looks exactly the same size and it arrives with the question of why you did not say so in week one. And the third one, which is the most expensive, is letting somebody else answer for you. The moment the founder goes quiet and the finance director takes over, the buyer starts pricing the company as if the founder were already gone. Sometimes that is what they wanted anyway. You just gave it to them for free.

We have been acquiring companies for eleven years now, and we have bought nine of them, so I can tell you what survives the data room and what does not. What does not survive is the story about culture. Every founder tells us they are different, that their people stay, that the culture is special. I believe them, mostly. But nothing in the documents supports it, so by week four it has quietly disappeared from the conversation and nobody mentions it again. What does survive is very simple. Something proprietary, which has been running in production long enough to prove that it actually works and not just that it demos well. And a founder who has been giving us the same answers since the first call. Consistency, over months, in a person, is the single thing I have paid a premium for and never regretted. Everything else we can rebuild.
